Volume 18 · Chapter 02

Resource allocation and institutional budgets

Professional Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v18-c01

By the endBuild budgets and allocate resources under opportunity cost and uncertainty.

Volume 18 · Chapter 2

Resource allocation and institutional budgets

Capability. Build dated operating and capital budgets, reconcile them to opening and closing financial positions, and defend resource choices when funds are restricted or uncertain. Read Institutional purpose and strategy, the statement connections, incremental capital budgeting and bank capital and liquidity. The two institutions, funding arrangements, accounting conventions and internal floors below are original synthetic teaching cases. They are not current legal, donor, tax, regulatory or accounting requirements.

1. A budget is a set of dated commitments and assumptions

A mission identifies what the institution values. A budget asks whether it can pay for the activities that serve that mission, when resources are needed and what it gives up. Begin with opening stocks, then identify each new flow and its date. A surplus for the full year does not pay a bill due before the associated receipt. Nor can an institution spend the same cash both to maintain a reserve and to acquire equipment.

An operating budget forecasts recurring revenues, costs and the resources required for services over an interval. A capital budget compares acquisitions or improvements whose consequences extend beyond the period, including their initial cash requirements and later incremental cash. A cash budget tracks receipts and payments at actual decision deadlines. A profit and loss statement, or P&L, recognizes revenues and expenses under declared conventions; an academic institution may instead report a change in net assets. These are related views, not interchangeable balances.

The SEC's dated introductory statement guide, retained from the accepted accounting chapter, supports the stock/flow and statement distinctions. It is not a current accounting standard. We supply every recognition rule used here. Depreciation allocates an already purchased asset's cost; it is not a second cash payment. A credit-loss provision changes the stipulated carrying value of loans and income without itself transferring cash. Borrowing raises cash and a liability, not revenue; an owner contribution raises cash and equity, not profit.

Committed funding has the required authorization and enforceable availability under the case's stated terms. An application, expected donation or desired credit line is an assumption until the relevant condition is met. Even an approved restricted grant may fund only eligible work. A budget must identify its holder, purpose, timing, permissions and uncertainty. A cash balance marked “restricted” cannot quietly become the unrestricted reserve because both accounts appear on the same consolidated statement.

Use a control equation at each date: closing cash equals opening cash plus actual available receipts less due payments. Use a separate position equation: assets equal liabilities plus equity or net assets. Reconcile closing equity to opening equity, recognized income and direct funding/distribution movements. A balanced equation can still use a wrong recognition rule or unsupported forecast; the reconciliation catches inconsistency but does not establish the truth of an input.

2. Value, permission and payment capacity answer different questions

For a supplied annual opportunity rate r>−1 and dated incremental cash flows C₀,…,Cₜ, NPV=ΣCₜ/(1+r)ᵗ, with the initial payment normally negative. Compare every alternative with the same feasible counterfactual. Include a foregone rental receipt if using owned space prevents it; exclude a past nonrefundable study when today's choice cannot change that payment. Do not subtract depreciation again from an already specified cash stream. With no taxes in our models there is no depreciation tax saving to insert.

The retained MIT capital-budgeting lectures provide the bounded incremental-cash and dated-value context. Our discount rates, project receipts and finite comparisons are assumptions proved here. A positive NPV does not supply upfront money, override a donor restriction or tell the institution which mission to adopt. Choose among feasible alternatives under the stated objective; report an infeasible mandate explicitly.

For an endowment, distinguish the invested stock from its permitted distribution. Here an endowment is a dedicated investment pool with a stipulated spending rule; this definition does not impose one legal treatment on every actual institution. Let opening value E₀ earn total return r and distribute D at period end. Then E₁=(1+r)E₀−D. The distribution is a transfer within a consolidated institution, so it is not new consolidated external revenue. A market loss can shrink the pool even if spending is zero. A percentage spending rule does not guarantee preservation of purchasing power.

If an institution wants E₁≥(1+π)E₀, where π is the period's inflation rate, algebra requires D≤E₀(r−π). For E₀>0, when r<π, no nonnegative distribution can meet that condition without additional contributions. This is a single-period identity under a specified return, not a universal optimal spending rule. Multi-year planning must address uncertain returns, restrictions, service continuity and what happens when targets conflict.

Scenario planning changes a coherent set of assumptions and recomputes the entire ledger. Name the base case, stress and decision rule before results arrive. A scenario is not a probability distribution unless probabilities are actually supplied. It is not a confidence interval or a forecast guarantee. Test dates as well as end-of-year totals, preserve the original assumptions and state what new evidence would justify changing them.

3. Two complete budget decisions

Case A — an institute cannot spend its consolidated wealth on any purpose

Scope and opening position. All amounts are thousands of currency units (kCU). The fictional Estuary Research Institute plans one year split into an upfront date0 and operating dates1 and2, where date2 is year end. It has unrestricted cash60, restricted research cash30, endowment investments200 and existing equipment with carrying amount40. There are no liabilities. Net assets330 comprise unrestricted100, research-restricted30 and endowment200. Opening tuple is (60,30,200,40,0). The restricted award was received and recognized before this opening date under this simplified case convention; do not recognize its cash or revenue again this year.

The approved research project requires cash expenditure12 at each operating date, all eligible against the30 restricted balance. Unspent6 remains restricted. Unrestricted operating cash expenses are50 at each date, comprising salaries80 and other costs20 for the year. All are recognized expenses when paid. Base external receipts, all earned and collected this year, are40 at date1 and60 at date2; the latter comprise58 service fees and2 rent from space available only if neither capital project uses it. There are no receivables, payables, taxes, borrowing, disposal proceeds or unlisted movements. A proposed next-year grant40 is unawarded and contributes zero to this year's available resources.

Existing equipment depreciation is8 for the year. The endowment's base total return is10, retained inside its investment value until its distribution at date2. The proposed rule permits distribution D=min{8,max{0,E₀+return−190}}: a4% opening-value cap and a190 nominal residual floor. The floor limits distribution; it does not insure investment losses. Under the base return, D8 is authorized for general operations and transferred into unrestricted cash only at date2. Internal policy requires unrestricted cash of at least20 at every listed deadline; restricted cash and undistributed endowment cannot satisfy that floor.

Case B — a lender's investment can add value and still need a smaller lending budget

Opening position and timing. All amounts are millions of currency units (mCU), for a different fictional entity, Cedar Lender. Cash50, gross loans160 less allowance8, and existing equipment18 give assets220. Deposits180 and equity40 fund them; no other liabilities exist. Opening tuple(cash,gross loans,allowance,equipment,deposits,equity) is (50,160,8,18,180,40). At date0 the lender can buy a processing system for12. At date1, withdrawals25 are paid, existing loan principal20 is collected and new loans20 are paid externally. These events are settled in the stated net block, with principal receipts available before new disbursements; the cash floor is tested after withdrawals as well as at each block end. At date2, interest16 is collected, deposit interest5 and operating cost8 are paid. No later inflow can be borrowed against unless expressly supplied.

Interest revenue is20: collected16 plus accrued receivable4. The accrual is collectible but not cash by date2. Loan provision6 increases the allowance from8 to14; there are no write-offs, recoveries or other loan changes. Depreciation6 comprises2 on existing equipment and4 on the new system. Tax, dividends, other comprehensive income and owner contributions are zero in the base case. These are stipulated recognition conventions, not an IFRS/GAAP or regulatory computation. All new loans begin earning after this planning year; their amount does not change the supplied current-year interest or provision on the original book.

The Bank of England's dated capital/liquidity primer, retained in its recorded conceptual scope, supports separating cash from loss-absorbing equity. Its historical rules and numerical thresholds are not used. Cedar's internal floors are cash≥10 at every stated payment checkpoint and closing equity≥32. Both must pass; adding their amounts is not a usable funding source.

Capital comparison. Without the system, current annual operating cost would be13 instead of8; all other base receipts, loan losses and opening resources are unchanged. The system saves5 at each of three year ends, costs12 now, has a three-year life and zero residual value, and creates no other cash, tax, capacity or working-capital change. The complete incremental stream is(−12,5,5,5). At the supplied10% opportunity rate its NPV is−12+5/(11/10)+5/(11/10)²+5/(11/10)³=578/1331. Capital tuple(cost,annual saving,life,rate) is (12,5,3,1/10); result 578/1331. The current-year depreciation charge4 on the system is not an additional cash cost in that calculation.

Repair with a real timing constraint. Suppose a separate revised authorization makes an owner contribution f available before the system purchase and permits new lending x between0 and20. Both are decision variables only within that revised authorization; wishing for equity is not funding. Keep the stress losses and interest assumptions fixed as stated. After purchase cash is38+f; after withdrawals it is3+f; after principal receipt and new lending it is23+f−x; year-end cash is22+f−x. Equity is31+f. The withdrawal checkpoint requires f≥7 even if x0, so shrinking later new loans alone cannot cure that earlier shortfall. This is why the actual event order matters.

A minimum feasible contribution is7, and then closing equity38 exceeds32 while x≤19 is required by year-end cash≥10. Choosing x19 maximizes lending among this authorized range: cash after purchase45, after withdrawals10, after principal/new loans11, at year end10. Gross loans159, allowance18, net loans141, equipment24 and receivable8 give assets183, equal deposits145 plus equity38. Repair tuple(f,x,cash after purchase,after withdrawal,after lending,year end,equity,net loans,assets) is (7,19,45,10,11,10,38,141,183). Funding1 would repair the equity floor but leave withdrawal cash4, six below its floor; no lending reduction fixes that prior payment.

Global feasibility proof. Given f≥0 and0≤x≤20, all constraints reduce to f≥7 and x≤min{20,12+f}: purchase cash38+f already passes; the withdrawal requires3+f≥10; the later lending checkpoint23+f−x≥10 is weaker than year-end22+f−x≥10; equity31+f≥32 is weaker than f≥7. Hence the region is necessary and sufficient for every stipulated checkpoint. At fixed authorized f7, x19 is the unique largest feasible new-loan amount; at f8, x20 fits with final10. A smaller contribution cannot be rescued by greater reported profit or a loan decision made after the withdrawal. No theorem about unmodeled intraday flows is claimed.

Complete treasury and allocation memorandum. “The processing system adds578/1331 modeled NPV relative to continued manual processing, but base P&L still loses5 and stress breaches both screens. Keep project value, annual income and dated funding separate. Treasury must document deposit withdrawal timing and usable contribution funds before commitment; the credit owner must reconcile original-book loss assumptions and the new-loan schedule. Under the stress and current ordering, request a specifically authorized7 equity contribution before date0 and cap new lending at19, contingent on actual receipt. Until that authorization and receipt exist, the repaired budget is a conditional proposal, not an executable approval. Preserve the original failed budget rather than replacing its stress with an optimistic forecast. The payment owner must stop if withdrawals exceed35 or expected interest receipts fall below12 without a revised feasible plan. Finance must reconcile the allowance, receivable, equipment and equity after actual results; a balanced forecast does not prove any of them.”

4. Make the budget an accountable decision record

A usable budget version identifies owner, period, units, opening stocks, each cash date, restrictions, assumptions, alternatives, approval status and decision triggers. Separate the forecast from the authorized ceiling and the actual ledger. When actuals depart from plan, distinguish volume, price, timing, recognition and scope changes before assigning responsibility. A late receipt may leave annual revenue unchanged while making a commitment infeasible; an asset loss may reduce equity without transferring cash that day.

Research funding deserves a specific commitment register. State award versus application, eligible costs, required matching resources, overhead treatment, payment/reimbursement dates, expiry and who bears an overrun. Our institute's research24 is already eligible and funded; a real proposal may require payroll before reimbursement or impose additional conditions. Do not assume a nominal award is immediately usable unrestricted cash. Preserve unfunded obligations and explicit deferrals; a rejected request is preferable to a fabricated balanced plan.

For each scenario, show what can still be changed at that date. Before a capital contract is signed, deferral may preserve liquidity. After an irrevocable purchase, that option disappears. An incremental value calculation should include the best still-feasible alternative, not one already unavailable. A new funder, collateral release or spending permission must be documented before entering the executable cash column. The budget supplies a reasoned proposal and a control process; real stewardship requires actual decisions and independent review over time.

Exercises

  1. Reconstruct all four closing assets and total net assets for Estuary's base X plan. Reconcile the total movement both from consolidated revenue/expenses and the three subfund movements. Explain why adding the endowment distribution as consolidated revenue is wrong.
  2. For X, calculate NPV if an analyst omits the foregone rent2 per year, then repair it. State the largest upfront cost c compatible with nonnegative NPV and separately with the base dated cash floor, holding receipts and life unchanged. Which ceiling binds first?
  3. Under Estuary's delay/return stress, prove the largest upfront expenditure compatible with the date1 floor, with no new funding and no change to base early operating receipts/expenses. Explain why year-end cash or the unawarded grant cannot resolve the early gap. Write a complete revised funding notice.
  4. Apply the endowment rule to total returns−20,−10,0,10. Report the allowed distribution and closing pool in each case. Prove the real-preservation spending bound and apply it at return5%, inflation2%. Explain what the nominal floor fails to guarantee.
  5. Reconcile Cedar's base profit to closing equity and its direct cash budget to the income-to-cash bridge. Compute the no-system base cash, equipment, profit and equity, keeping manual operating expense13 and only existing depreciation2. Explain why a positive project NPV is compatible with an annual institutional loss.
  6. Under Cedar's stress, a manager offers owner funding1 and cuts new lending to13. Recompute every cash checkpoint and equity. Does this satisfy the stated floors? Then give the minimum funding and maximum lending at that funding under the actual event order, with a full balance sheet.
  7. Change only the stress event order so that principal20 is actually received before the withdrawal35; receipts are unencumbered and available at that earlier moment. Derive the new feasible funding/lending region and the largest lending with funding1. Explain the documentary evidence required before using this revised ordering.
  8. Write a full committee review of this proposed report: “Estuary has enough consolidated assets, so move the research reserve into equipment; its draw8 is new income and its grant application40 funds the delay. Cedar's positive system NPV proves the stress plan is affordable; just add cash and equity as the total buffer.” Correct every error, name the required owners and supply a concrete conditional decision for each institution.
Complete solutions and evaluation criteria

1. One entity, three fund records

Cash is58 unrestricted and6 restricted; investments202; equipment44; assets310, liabilities0 and net assets310. Consolidated external income114+10=124 minus cash operating expense124 and depreciation20 yields−20. The subfund changes are unrestricted+2, research−24 and endowment+2, summing−20. Opening330 therefore closes310. Distribution8 reduces endowment assets and increases unrestricted cash; neither the institution's total assets nor its external income rises from that transfer. Counting it as revenue without the corresponding internal elimination would falsely report change−12 and ending net assets318. Tuple(correct closing,false closing) is (310,318). Full credit requires every asset, both reconciliations and the internal-transfer explanation.

2. Opportunity cost and a separate payment ceiling

The erroneous value is−24+16/(11/10)+16/(11/10)²=456/121. The foregone rent has present value2/(11/10)+2/(11/10)²=420/121, leaving36/121. The value ceiling for c is14·210/121=2940/121. Dated unrestricted cash is60−c at date0,50−c at date1 and82−c at year end; the20 floor requires c≤40, c≤30 and c≤62 respectively, so the funding ceiling is30. The NPV ceiling2940/121 is smaller than30 and binds first. Results(wrong NPV,foregone rent PV,value ceiling,cash ceiling) are (456/121,420/121,2940/121,30). The sunk study3 remains excluded. Credit the with/without stream, all cash dates and distinct ceilings; the new equipment's depreciation changes with cost but does not change this no-tax cash analysis.

3. A late receipt cannot pay an early obligation

With upfront expenditure c≥0, date1 cash is60−c+20−50=30−c. The floor20 requires c≤10; date0's c≤40 is weaker. A purchase24 misses by14, even though X's year-end cash50 passes. No new funding is available in the stated stress; the grant application40 is not an award or receipt, and research cash has a different permitted purpose. Result(capital ceiling,gap for X) is (10,14).

Notice: “Finance will defer X before an irrevocable commitment and retain the rental use, giving date1 unrestricted cash30. Preserve the research12+12 plan and its unspent restricted6; the research lead must verify eligible obligations independently of the general cash shortage. The investment overseer will authorize draw0 under the return stress. Any alternative X approval requires at least14 additional usable cash before date1, with documented source, conditions and later repayment obligations if borrowed; none is assumed here. Record the delay as timing uncertainty, not lower earned annual income.” Full credit requires the bound, honest available-funding status and complete owner/action notice; a different feasible revision must provide its entire dated ledger.

4. A cap does not insure the pool

For returns−20,−10,0,10, the distribution/closing pairs are(0,180),(0,190),(8,192),(8,202): ((0,180),(0,190),(8,192),(8,202)). At loss20, zero spending cannot maintain190; the formula avoids making the loss worse through distributions but does not create missing assets. From E₁=(1+r)E₀−D≥(1+π)E₀, subtract E₀ and rearrange to D≤E₀(r−π). At5% return and2% inflation, bound6; draw8 leaves202 versus required204, a shortfall2. If r<π, even D0 fails without contributions; if r=π, D0 meets exactly. Credit all regimes, the global algebra and the distinction between a nominal distribution condition and real wealth preservation. The rule does not establish a sustainable multi-year spending policy.

5. Project value is incremental and multi-period

Base profit20−5−8−6−6=−5; equity40−5=35. Cash bridge−5+6+6−4=3, then3−12−25+20−20=−34, so50−34=16. Without the system, cash ends50−25+20−20+16−5−13=23; equipment18−2=16; profit20−5−13−6−2=−6 and equity34. Net loans146 and receivable4 are unchanged; assets23+146+16+4=189=deposits155+equity34. No-system tuple(cash,equipment,profit,equity,assets) is (23,16,-6,34,189). The system reduces first-year cash by7 (purchase12 less saving5) and improves income by1 (saving5 less extra depreciation4). NPV578/1331 compares the complete three-year incremental stream, whereas loss5 is the whole institution's current-year recognized result. Full credit requires both reconciliations and their boundaries.

6. Funding equity alone does not fund an earlier withdrawal

With f1,x13 under the actual order, cash after purchase39, after withdrawal4, after principal/new loans11 and at year end10. Equity32 passes, but withdrawal cash4 violates10 by6. Result (39,4,11,10,32,6). The first checkpoint after withdrawal forces f≥7 irrespective of x. At f7, year-end cash29−x≥10 implies x≤19, while all other conditions pass. Thus minimum funding7 and largest lending at that funding19. Closing cash10, gross loans159, allowance18, equipment24 and receivable8 produce assets183; deposits145 and equity38 reconcile them. These are conditional revised resources, not funds already available in the original plan. Full credit requires the failed intermediate checkpoint, necessary/sufficient constraints and entire closing position; testing only year-end cash earns no timing credit.

7. A genuinely earlier receipt changes the feasible set

After purchase cash38+f, after principal receipt58+f, after withdrawal23+f, after new lending23+f−x and at year end22+f−x. With f≥0,0≤x≤20, early checkpoints automatically pass. Equity requires f≥1; final cash requires x≤12+f and is tighter than the post-lending checkpoint. Hence necessary and sufficient region is f≥1 and0≤x≤min{20,12+f}. At f1 choose x13; checkpoints39,59,24,11,10 and equity32 all pass. Closing gross loans153 less allowance18 gives net135; equipment24 and receivable8, so assets10+135+24+8=177=deposits145+equity32. Result (1,13,39,59,24,11,10,32,135,177).

“Treasury must provide a dated, enforceable settlement schedule showing the20 principal receipt clears and is usable before the withdrawal; an expected receipt later that day is insufficient. The payment owner and independent reviewer must confirm availability and absence of restrictions, preserve the old order and explain the change before approving this smaller contribution. If the evidence fails, restore the original f≥7 constraint.” Credit the complete changed-order proof, numerical reconciliation and actual evidence requirement. A different timing assumption is a different feasible problem, not an arithmetic repair to the old one.

8. A complete accountable correction

“Estuary's consolidated assets include equipment, restricted research cash and a dedicated investment pool; they are not all general payment capacity. Finance and the research lead must preserve eligible project spending12 at each date and its6 restricted remainder. Distribution8 is an internal transfer, and the application40 supplies no committed funding. Under the given delay and return stress, the investment overseer applies draw0; defer X before purchase and retain rental use, leaving unrestricted cash30 at date1 and60 at year end. Any replacement funding must be authorized and actually usable before the binding payment; do not use the projected year-end balance to approve an earlier shortfall.

“Cedar's system has positive incremental NPV578/1331 under the supplied three-year forecasts, while the original stress leaves withdrawal cash3 and equity31 below internal floors. Cash is already an asset funded by deposits and equity; adding equity to cash double-counts a claim rather than producing a payment resource. Treasury must secure documented owner funding7 before purchase and limit new lending to19 under the original event order, conditional on actual authorization and receipt; otherwise return the proposal as infeasible and revise commitments before they become irrevocable. Credit and finance must preserve the stress provision10, interest collection12 and receivable8. Reordering principal receipts requires separate verified settlement evidence, not managerial preference. Each committee must retain original/revised budgets, named approvals and a stop condition for worse receipts or withdrawals. These are conditional fictional decisions, not claims that real institutional leadership occurred.” Full credit requires all five report errors, accurate quantitative replacements, ownership and a genuinely conditional implementation record.

Teach-back and delayed retention

Teach-back. Explain why an endowment draw is usable operating cash but not consolidated external income, why depreciation changes income but not the current equipment payment, and why positive NPV cannot repair a missed payment checkpoint. Guide: identify the entity boundary, the original asset payment and the dated available funding; use Estuary's8 transfer, Cedar's4 new depreciation and its withdrawal checkpoint.

Delayed transfer. In Estuary's base case keep X but lower the early receipt from40 to34, shifting6 to year end; then lower it to33. Full answer: date1 cash20 then19, so the first meets the floor and the second misses by1; annual cash58 is unchanged because receipts only move dates. For Cedar's original stress order, authorize f8 and set x20. Full answer: after purchase46, after withdrawal11, after principal/new lending11, year-end10 and equity39. The boundary tuple is (20,19,58,46,11,11,10,39). A correct published key is not evidence the learner retained the reasoning; record actual unaided work after a gap.

Sources, limits and continuation

The three primary source routes are reused only within their retained inspection scopes: dated statement education, incremental capital budgeting and the conceptual cash/equity distinction. No fresh source-body inspection, current institutional spending policy, legal permission or comprehensive accounting compliance is claimed. All numerical budgets, decision memoranda, recognition conventions and proofs are original. Real institutions need contract-specific restrictions, multiple currencies, taxes, uncertain project demand, funding costs and finer cash deadlines beyond these cases. Organizations, incentives and culture examines how responsibilities and rewards influence whether an approved resource plan serves its purpose.

Sources and further study

  • U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (2007), Beginners' Guide to Financial Statement — Dated investor-education orientation to balance sheets, income statements, cash-flow statements, equity changes and explanatory notes. Harbor's recognition conventions and numerical cases are original and separately stipulated.
  • Andrew W. Lo, MIT 15.401 Finance Theory I — Lectures 18–20: Capital Budgeting (2007–2008) — NPV choice, incremental after-tax cash and working capital, project interactions, IRR limitations and risk/date matching.
  • Marc Farag, Damian Harland and Dan Nixon — Bank capital and liquidity (Bank of England Quarterly Bulletin, 2013 Q3, pp. 201–215) — Historical UK central-bank conceptual primer for bank balance-sheet funding, equity versus deployable cash, valuation bases and high-level ratio denominators. Original chapter ledger, definitions, calculations and exercises supply their own assumptions.
